body.title: From Vijayanagara to Madurai: an empire and a temple city
body.summary: The empire ruled from Hampi rebuilt Madurai's great temple, and Madurai's Nayak rulers began as its viceroys.

rationale.text: After the Meenakshi Temple was destroyed in the fourteenth century, it was rebuilt by the Vijayanagara Empire, whose capital was at Hampi.
The Madurai Nayak dynasty was founded around 1529 as a viceroyalty under the Vijayanagara Empire, and Nayak commanders serving the empire expanded the temple.

whyItMatters.text: It shows how political authority moved across South India and how temple-building was bound up with that authority, linking a ruined capital in Karnataka to a living temple city in Tamil Nadu.

body.doesNotEstablish: This political relationship does not by itself show that Madurai's architecture copies Hampi's, or that the temple's religious meaning derives from Vijayanagara. Architectural influence would need its own evidence.

claims.text: The Meenakshi Temple was rebuilt by the Vijayanagara Empire in the 14th century after its destruction.

evidence.excerpt: It was later rebuilt by the Vijayanagara Empire in the 14th century, after its destruction by the armies of the Delhi Sultanate.

claims.text: Hampi was the Vijayanagara capital from 1336 to 1565.

evidence.excerpt: Hampi was the capital of the Vijayanagara (Karnata) Empire from 1336 to 1565 (as Vijayanagara), when it was abandoned.

claims.text: The Madurai Nayak dynasty was founded around 1529 as a viceroyalty under Vijayanagara.

evidence.excerpt: It was founded by Nagama Nayak's son Viswanatha Nayak around 1529 as a viceroyalty under the Vijayanagara Empire.

claims.text: Nayak commanders serving the Vijayanagara empire expanded the temple.

evidence.excerpt: The Nayak commanders, who served under the Vijayanagara empire, expanded the temple further.
